sources.citation: Klar, Kathryn A. 1992. John P. Harrington's phonetic representations of Obispeño Chumash palatal consonants. In James E. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress; discusses Harrington's two 'long s' graphs = č vs. palatalized t^y, evidence for two Obispeño dialects in Rosario Cooper's speech, and mentions an unpublished 'brief grammatical sketch of Obispeño' in Harrington's hand at the NAA.

sources.citation: Klar, Kathryn A. 1977. Topics in Historical Chumash Grammar. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. 194 pp. (eScholarship item 31t2k96m).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Chapter 'Correspondences and Reconstructions I: The Proto-Chumash Phonological Inventory' (diss. pp.10-32 = PDF pp.13-35) gives the Obispeño consonant and vowel inventory (pp.12-13), aspiration/gemination rules, the Obispeño t^y/q split and vowel ablaut; full-document scanned has zero hits for stress/accent/penult/syllable and the cited Obispeño forms carry no stress marks.

sources.citation: Heizer, Robert F. (ed.) 1955. California Indian linguistic records: The Mission Indian vocabularies of H. W. Henshaw. Anthropological Records 15(2):85-202.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No rule; the Phonetic Key states 'The accented syllable of every word marked by an acute accent', so Henshaw's 1884 San Luis Obispo vocabulary (MS 852a, speaker Alikano) is accent-marked raw data from which stress position could be tallied.
